mcqs.question: To find the Kth largest element in a stream using a fixed-size-K heap, why do you keep a min-heap rather than a max-heap?
options: A max-heap can't be capped at a fixed size
Min-heaps are always faster to implement in every language
It doesn't matter which you choose, both work identically
The root needs to be the smallest of the current top-K, which is exactly the Kth largest value, and a min-heap gives O(1) access to that
mcqs.explanation: The heap holds the K largest values seen so far, and the boundary value you actually want — the Kth largest — is the smallest one in that set, which sits at a min-heap's root. A max-heap's root would give you the single largest value, not the Kth.

mcqs.question: For the top-K frequent elements problem, why does the heap phase run in O(m log k) where m is the number of distinct elements, rather than O(n log k) where n is the total input size?
options: The heap only processes a random sample of the input
A counting pass first collapses duplicates into a frequency map, so the heap only ever sees one entry per distinct element
m and n are always equal for this problem
The heap uses a different, faster algorithm when duplicates are present
mcqs.explanation: The count-first phase is a separate O(n) pass that reduces n raw values down to m distinct (value, frequency) pairs; only those m pairs ever get pushed into the heap, so the heap's cost scales with the number of distinct elements, not the total input length.

mcqs.question: You need the single Kth largest element of a static, fully in-memory array, computed once, and you don't mind a rare worst case. Which approach is typically fastest on average?
options: A size-K heap, since it's always faster than any comparison-based approach
Sorting the whole array, since it's the simplest and most predictable
Quickselect, since it achieves O(n) average time by partitioning rather than fully sorting or maintaining a heap
None of these — Kth-element queries require O(n log n) no matter the approach
mcqs.explanation: Quickselect's partition-based approach only needs to narrow down to the Kth position, not fully order the array or maintain a running structure, giving O(n) average time — better than the heap's O(n log k) or a full sort's O(n log n) for a single one-shot query on static data. It does have an O(n²) worst case, which median-of-medians can bound away at more implementation cost.

mcqs.question: An implementation pushes every element from an n-item input into an unbounded heap, then pops K times at the end to get the top-K. Is this correct, and what's the cost?
options: It's incorrect — it produces the wrong K elements
It's correct, but it costs O(n log n), giving up the entire benefit of capping the heap at size K
It's correct and costs the same O(n log k) as the capped-heap approach
It's correct and actually faster than the size-K heap approach
mcqs.explanation: This gives the right answer but pays to maintain a heap over the full input, which is O(n log n) — no better than sorting. The entire value of the pattern is capping the heap at size K throughout, so every heap operation costs O(log k), not O(log n).

mcqs.question: For "K closest points to the origin" using a fixed-size-K heap ordered by distance, why is a max-heap used instead of a min-heap?
options: Distance values are always negative, requiring a max-heap
The point that must be evicted when the heap overflows is the farthest kept point, and a max-heap's root gives O(1) access to that
Max-heaps are faster to construct than min-heaps in general
Min-heaps cannot be ordered by a computed key like distance
mcqs.explanation: The rule is that the heap's root is always whatever you're about to evict; since you keep the closest points and discard the farthest one on overflow, the farthest (max) needs to be at the root, which requires a max-heap ordered by distance.

mcqs.question: In the fixed-size-K heap pattern, what's the correct order of operations when a new candidate arrives?
options: Check the heap size first; only push if there's room, otherwise discard the new candidate
Pop the current worst element first to make room, then push the new candidate unconditionally
Push the new candidate first, then check the size and pop if it now exceeds K
Push and pop simultaneously in a single atomic heap operation
mcqs.explanation: Pushing first lets the heap correctly decide, via a normal comparison, whether the new candidate actually deserves to stay — popping before pushing risks evicting a valid member to make room for a candidate that turns out to be worse than everything already kept.
